content_blocks.text: Debugging Dart Code in an IDE matters because Dart programs need predictable behavior, explicit contracts, and examples that can be verified. This topic focuses on breakpoints, stepping, variable inspection, and watch expressions. Keep the lesson’s core distinction separate from runtime, SDK, package, or platform details that may vary. When you build on this idea, state your assumptions, try the smallest useful example, and check edge cases before integrating it into a larger project.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Run several times and treat timings as observations, not guarantees; use a profiler for real workloads.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet, rerun the same command, and compare the complete output. For package/platform examples, restore pubspec and target settings too.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or condition in the example for “Debugging Dart Code in an IDE”. Predict the output first, then run or statically inspect it. Add one boundary test and explain why the result is expected.

Common mistakes: confusing a language guarantee with a runtime or package behavior; skipping malformed/empty inputs; relying on undocumented version assumptions; and changing multiple things before reproducing a failure. Prefer explicit naming, a small test, and official documentation.
